concept.title: Troubleshooting
concept.shortdesc: Use a systematic troubleshooting process to identify and correct Internet, Wi-Fi, signal, and client-device connection problems.

section.title: Overview
section.p: A network problem can occur in the ISP service, the , the , the wireless connection, or a client device.
Identify the affected devices and test each part of the network before you change the network configuration.
section.note: Start with the physical connections and status indicators. Make one change at a time. Test the connection after each change.
Record the symptoms, affected devices, network path, assigned addresses, signal conditions, and configuration changes before you modify the network.

section.title: Identify the Problem
section.p: Collect information about the problem before you start troubleshooting.
Determine the following information:

ul.li: When the problem started
Whether the problem affects one device or all connected devices
Whether the problem affects wired devices, wireless devices, or both
Whether the device can access the local network
Whether the device can access Internet services
Whether the device remains connected to
Whether the problem occurs in one location or throughout the coverage area
Whether the problem started after a configuration, firmware, hardware, or location change

section.note: Do not change several settings at the same time. Multiple changes can make the cause of the problem difficult to identify.

section.title: Troubleshooting Sequence
section.p: Check the network in the following sequence:

ol.li: Check the power and cable connections.
Check the status indicators on the and .
Check the connection between the and the on the .
Check the Ethernet or Wi-Fi connection on the client device.
Verify access to the .
Verify local network access.
Verify Internet access.
Review the client device on the .
Review the applicable Wi-Fi, security, and network settings.
Restart the affected devices if the connections and settings are correct.

section.note: Complete the checks in the specified sequence. Stop when the connection operates correctly.
Isolate the fault by testing each network boundary separately: client to router, router to modem or ONT, and modem or ONT to the ISP.

section.title: Physical Connection Checks
section.p: Make sure that each network device is connected to power and is turned on.
Make sure that the Ethernet cable from the or ONT is connected to the on the .
For a wired client device, make sure that the Ethernet cable is connected to an available LAN port. Check each cable for loose connectors or visible damage.
section.note: Do not use a damaged power adapter, power cable, or Ethernet cable. Replace a damaged component with an approved component.
Do not look into an optical port or the end of a fiber-optic cable. Contact the ISP if the fiber connection requires service.

section.title: Status Indicator Checks
section.p: Check the power, Internet, WAN, LAN, and Wi-Fi status indicators on the applicable network devices.
A status indicator that is off or shows an error can identify the affected connection.
section.note: Indicator names, colors, and patterns can differ by device. Refer to the instructions supplied with the device.
Compare the current indicator state with the normal operating state before you restart or reset a device.

section.title: Determine the Scope of the Problem
section.p: Test another client device on the same network.
If only one device has the problem, check that device and its network settings. If all devices have the problem, check the router, modem or ONT, and ISP service.
If wired devices operate correctly but wireless devices do not, check the Wi-Fi settings and wireless environment.
If wireless devices operate correctly in one location but not in another, check the router location, signal strength, and physical obstructions.

strow.stentry: Client-device settings, saved Wi-Fi information, and device software
Router, modem or ONT, ISP service, and network configuration
SSID, password, security mode, band, channel, and interference
Ethernet cables, LAN ports, and client Ethernet settings
Signal strength, distance, physical obstructions, and interference
Local network operates, but Internet access fails
WAN connection, modem or ONT, ISP service, gateway, and DNS

section.title: Local Network Check
section.p: Connect a client device to the through Ethernet or .
Open in a supported web browser. If the sign-in page opens, the client device can communicate with the router.
section.note: Access to the router sign-in page verifies the local network connection. It does not verify Internet access.
If the sign-in page does not open, verify the client IP address, subnet mask, and default gateway before you change the router configuration.

section.title: Internet Connection Check
section.p: Open a trusted external website from a connected client device.
If the router sign-in page opens but the external website does not open, the local network is operating, but Internet access is not available.
Check the connection between the and the . Check the Internet service status supplied by the ISP.
section.note: Verify that the client device has a valid default gateway and DNS server. Test gateway connectivity separately from DNS name resolution.

section.title: Network Settings Check
section.p: Sign in to the and open the .
Confirm that the client device appears in the list of connected devices. Review the connection type, device name, IP address, and signal information when available.
section.note: If the device uses automatic network configuration, confirm that the assigned a valid address. The assigned address is typically in .
Confirm that the client device uses and when the network uses the default addressing configuration from this guide.
The network can use different address values if an administrator changed the default configuration.

section.title: Restart Network Devices
section.p: Restart the network devices if the physical connections and network settings are correct, but the problem continues.
Use the following restart sequence:

ol.li: Turn off the client device.
Turn off the .
Turn off the or ONT if the ISP permits this action.
Wait for the devices to turn off completely.
Turn on the or ONT.
Wait until the Internet service indicator shows normal operation.
Turn on the .
Wait until the router status indicators show normal operation.
Turn on the client device.
Test the network connection.

section.note: Restarting a device and resetting a device are different actions. A restart does not remove the saved configuration. A factory reset can remove all custom settings.
Do not perform a factory reset unless the applicable troubleshooting topic or the instructs you to do so.

section.title: Recent Configuration Changes
section.p: Review changes that were made before the problem started.
Examples include:

ul.li: A changed Wi-Fi network name or password
A changed wireless security mode
A changed Wi-Fi band, channel, or channel width
A router or client-device firmware update
A new access point or mesh node
A moved router, access point, or client device
A new appliance or wireless device
A changed DHCP or IP address configuration
A changed guest or IoT network setting

section.p: Reverse only the applicable change and test the network again.
section.note: Do not restore an old configuration if the configuration contains insecure settings or known errors.

section.title: Select a Troubleshooting Topic
section.p: Select the topic that matches the observed problem.

strow.stentry: Connected devices cannot access the Internet
The Wi-Fi connection is slower than expected
The Wi-Fi signal is weak in one or more areas
The network connection stops and starts
One client device cannot connect to the network
